This is the 12-bar blues from the bass player's chair, starting from one note per chord. You
need to know how to fret a note and pluck it. Everything else is built here, one step at a
time. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see
[Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues](blues-changes.qmd).

**How to use the page.** Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button
that starts the band. The diagrams read like a bass standing upright in front of you: the
low E string is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets.
Click a chord's name above a diagram to hear its notes. Under the diagrams the same notes
are written on a staff, and below the chord chart is the bass line the band is playing. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, the bar on
the chart and the diagram of the chord being played both light up. Tick **Leave out the
bass** and the band's bass player stops so that you can take the part. The strip at the
bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.

## 1. The roots

The **root** is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. A blues has three
chords, so it has three roots, and they sit close together. Find the key note on the E
string. The root of the **IV** chord is at the same fret on the next string up. The root of
the **V** chord is two frets higher on that same string. Your hand does not have to move.


In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the
diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of **V** is at the same fret on
the lowest string and the root of **IV** is two frets below that.

Start with two notes in each bar, on beats 1 and 3.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="roots" data-bass="halves"></div>

Count the bars as you play: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. When that is
steady, play the root on every beat. Press **Superimposed** to see all three roots on one
fretboard.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="roots" data-bass="roots" data-view="super"></div>

## 2. Root, fifth and octave

The **fifth** of a chord is one string up and two frets up from its root. The **octave**
(the root again, higher) is two strings up and two frets up. Index finger on the root, ring
or little finger on the other two: the three notes make a box that has the same shape on
every chord. Move the box to each root you learned in step 1.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="fifth" data-bass="alt"></div>

The band's bass plays root on beat 1 and fifth on beat 3. Play that first, then try
root, fifth, octave, fifth, one note to a beat.

## 3. The 3rd and the 7th

The root and fifth say which chord it is but not what *kind* of chord. Two other notes do
that job.

- The **3rd** says major or minor. In a dominant seventh chord (G7) it is a major 3rd: one
  string up and one fret *back* from the root.
- The **7th** in a blues chord is a flat 7th (written ♭7), a whole step below the octave: two
  strings up at the *same fret* as the root.

Together they are called the **guide tones**, because they are the notes that change the
most tellingly from one chord to the next. Root, 3rd, 5th and ♭7th are the four **chord
tones**. Click each chord's name to hear them climb.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="tones" data-bass="arp"></div>

### Where the flat 7 comes from

Why is the 7th of these chords called *flat*? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to
hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the
bottom.

<div class="bl-scale"></div>

The band's bass plays exactly that: root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7th, one note on every beat, the same
shape in every bar. The line is written out below the chord chart. It is not a walking line
yet. It is the four chord tones in order, so that your hand learns each shape and your ear
learns what each note sounds like against its chord.

Work up to it in three stages, each for a few choruses:

1. Root on beat 1, 3rd on beat 3. Two notes to a bar.
2. Root, 3rd, 5th, and rest on beat 4.
3. All four notes, as the band plays them.

Then switch to **Superimposed** and look at I and IV together. The
3rd of the I chord is one fret below the root of IV, and the ♭7th of I is one fret above the
3rd of IV. Those half steps are how the chords connect.

## 4. Walking

In step 3 every bar went the same way: up the chord from the root. A walking line also has
one note on every beat, but it chooses its notes so that each bar *leads into the next*.
Three changes turn the step 3 line into a walking line: the notes after the root can come
in any order, the octave joins them, and the last note of the bar points at the next root.
A recipe that always works:

1. **Beat 1**: the root of the chord.
2. **Beats 2 and 3**: any two other chord tones (3rd, 5th, ♭7th, or the octave).
3. **Beat 4**: an *approach note*, one fret below or one fret above the root of the *next*
   bar's chord.

When the next bar is the same chord, beat 4 can be any chord tone. The diagram shows the
chord tones of all three chords at once. A split dot is a note two chords share.

Between the chord tones you can also step along the scale that goes with the chord. Over
the I chord that is the scale from step 3, the major scale with its 7th lowered a half step
(called Mixolydian). Here it is in one place on the neck, with the run written in tablature.
Beats 2 and 3 can borrow its notes, so a bar can climb step by step instead of jumping.

<div class="bl-notes" data-scale="mixolydian" data-on="I"></div>

<div class="bl-step" data-part="walk" data-bass="walk" data-view="super"></div>

Listen to the band's bass player for a chorus, then tick **Leave out the bass** and walk it
yourself. Slow the tempo down as far as you need. A plain line that lands on the root at
every chord change is worth more than a busy one that does not.

## 5. The jazz blues

The last line of a jazz blues is a **two-five**: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8
to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of
[the changes lesson](blues-changes.qmd)). The ii chord is a **minor seventh** chord. Its
3rd is a *minor* 3rd, three frets above the root on the same string. Everything else about
the shape stays the same.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="tones" data-chart="jazz" data-show="Gm7 C7 F7 D7" data-bass="walk" data-view="super"></div>

In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Play the root on the beat each chord
arrives and one other note after it: root and 3rd, or root and an approach note into the
next root.

## 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet

Oscar Pettiford, who wrote this tune, was a bass player. Its changes are the three-chord
blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12 to turn it round. The melody
is one two-bar riff played three times, so the bass has room to be heard.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="walk" data-chart="closet" data-tune="closet" data-show="F7 Bb7 Gm7 C7" data-bass="walk" data-view="super"></div>

Play roots through the form first, two to a bar, and listen to how the riff sits against
them. Then walk it. In bars 4 and 8 the melody holds one long note: that is the place for
your line to lead clearly into the next chord. In bar 12, aim for the root of the V chord
and then back to the top.

## Where to go next

- Change the key in the strip at the bottom and find the same shapes in the new place.
  Start with F, B♭, A and E.
- Loop a chorus with the bass left out and record yourself over the band.
- Learn to improvise over the same tune in [the improvising lesson](blues-improv.qmd).
- Take any chorus from [the changes lesson](blues-changes.qmd) and walk through it with
  the recipe from step 4.
- Next on bass: [pop changes for bass](pop-changes-bass.qmd), roots and the walking line.
